Surgical · Breast implants

Silicone Breast Implants: A Patient Guide

Silicone gel-filled breast implants are medical devices with an outer shell and a silicone gel filling. They are different from injectable silicone, which must never be represented as an equivalent or safe substitute for an implant.

Home/Surgical/Silicone implants

Not the same as injectable silicone

Injectable silicone is a different product and should not be used as a substitute for a breast implant. Injectable silicone used for breast enhancement can cause serious, potentially permanent harm.

How implant selection works

Implant selection depends on individual anatomy, product characteristics, surgical assessment and the patient’s preferences. Patients should receive the relevant product information and understand that breast implants are not lifetime devices.

Additional operations may be needed, and complications can include rupture, capsular contracture, infection, changes in sensation and other implant-associated risks.

Verify before publishing

Only implant brands, models and regulatory claims that the clinic can verify should be published. Specific brand names are intentionally omitted here until verified.

Implant data from the American Society of Plastic Surgeons

  • Silicone gel implants feel more like natural breast tissue and do not collapse if the shell leaks; saline implants contain sterile salt water and collapse and are absorbed or expelled if they leak.
  • The FDA approves saline implants from age 18 and silicone implants from age 22.
  • For silicone implants, the FDA recommends screening with MRI or ultrasound five to six years after placement and every two to three years thereafter.
  • Breast implants are not guaranteed to last a lifetime; future surgery may be needed to replace one or both implants.
  • ASPS lists BIA-ALCL and BIA-SCC among the very rare cancers that can occur in the capsule around an implant, and notes that textured implants are where BIA-ALCL occurs most often.
  • Some patients report systemic symptoms (fatigue, “brain fog”, muscle or joint pain and rash) that they attribute to implants and which are commonly referred to as breast implant illness (BII).
